analysis.one_liner: Gives the FTC stronger tools to investigate and stop consumer fraud, especially telemarketing fraud targeting seniors.
analysis.headline: The Consumer Fraud Prevention Act never left the Senate Commerce Committee, despite a subcommittee holding hearings on it in May 1990.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have expanded the Federal Trade Commission's power to fight consumer fraud. It would have made false advertising for services illegal (current law only covered products), let the FTC subpoena physical evidence, tap postal records, and freeze fraudsters' financial accounts before the money disappears. It also would have extended mail-order consumer protections to telemarketing, let state attorneys general help enforce FTC rules, and required studies of life care homes and long-term care insurance sales to seniors.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, especially senior citizens, who the bill's findings say are defrauded more often than other consumers and lose billions of dollars a year to telemarketing and health fraud. Honest businesses in all fields, which the bill says are undermined when fraudulent competitors operate. State attorneys general, who would gain a formal role enforcing FTC rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, especially seniors, and honest businesses

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to spread false advertisements meant to induce the purchase of services, closing a loophole in the FTC Act that only covered false ads for products.

Gives the FTC new investigative powers: subpoenaing physical evidence like medical devices and drug products, accessing Postal Service mail cover reports like other law enforcement agencies, and getting court-ordered access to fraud suspects' financial records when the money is likely to be moved or destroyed.

Lets courts join parties with common interests in false advertising suits and lets the FTC serve process anywhere in the country, targeting fraud rings that dodge prosecution by scattering across states and using fake legal entities.

Requires the FTC to extend its mail-order rule to telemarketing within 270 days, and to consider requiring telemarketers to tell consumers they are entitled to refunds if goods are not delivered on time, plus a three-day cancellation right for prize-solicitation sales.
Allows the FTC to appoint state attorneys general to help enforce its rules, and requires the FTC to respond to their requests within 15 days.
Requires FTC studies and reports to Congress on deceptive practices in the life care home industry and in the marketing of long-term care insurance to the elderly.

analysis.who_pays: Fraudulent telemarketers and deceptive advertisers, who would face new liability, expanded investigations, and a rule presuming they are in violation if they keep inadequate compliance records. Legitimate telemarketing and mail-order businesses would bear compliance costs, including recordkeeping to prove they meet refund and delivery rules.

drawbacks.text: The bill expands government surveillance and data access: it gives the FTC access to Postal Service mail cover records and to consumers' financial records through courts, which civil liberties-minded lawmakers often question even when aimed at fraud.

The telemarketing rule imposes compliance and recordkeeping costs on all telemarketers, and includes a presumption that a telemarketer with inadequate records is in violation, a burden that falls on legitimate sellers as well as fraudsters.
The bill explicitly shields banks and payment processors from telemarketer liability, so financial institutions that process payments for fraudulent sales would not be on the hook.

The bill's most concrete near-term deliverables for the two areas it singles out — life care homes and long-term care insurance — are only studies and reports, not new rules, so no protection for seniors in those markets would arrive quickly even if enacted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad but diffuse: stronger anti-fraud enforcement against schemes that the bill's own findings say cost Americans billions annually and fall hardest on seniors. The costs are real but modest — compliance costs for legitimate telemarketers and mail-order sellers, and expanded government data access requiring court oversight. The main design weakness is that the two industries the bill scrutinizes most closely, life care homes and long-term care insurance, would only get studies rather than rules. On balance this is a conventional, moderate consumer-protection enforcement bill.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, a subcommittee held hearings on it, and then it sat until the Congress ended without ever getting a committee vote or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. John McCain introduced the bill on July 31, 1989, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
On May 2, 1990, the Senate Consumer Subcommittee held hearings on the bill, which were printed as S.Hrg. 101-765.
The bill never advanced past the committee stage: it received no committee vote, no floor vote, and expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
The bill had no cosponsors at any point.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fraudulent telemarketers and deceptive advertisers are better off, since the enforcement tools and refund rules aimed at them never became law. Consumers — especially seniors targeted by health fraud and telemarketing scams — are left with the same protections they had before.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so the record shows no clear partisan pattern; the bill's sole sponsor was a Republican and the committee that held it was run by Democrats.

industries.note: The bill would have extended mail-order refund and delivery rules to telemarketing, imposed disclosure and cancellation requirements, and presumed violators guilty of breaking the rule if they kept poor records. The bill's findings estimate telemarketing fraud costs consumers billions of dollars a year.

Legitimate mail-order sellers would face new compliance costs as the rule they already follow expanded to phone sales, while honest sellers also stood to benefit from a rule that the bill says undermines legitimate commerce.

The bill expressly carves out financial institutions and payment-system participants from telemarketer liability, shielding them from responsibility for processing payments for fraudulent phone sales.
The bill would have ordered an FTC study of unfair or deceptive practices in life care homes, potentially leading to new regulation, but imposed no immediate requirements.
The bill would have ordered a study of deceptive marketing of long-term care policies to the elderly and how premiums compare to claims paid, but imposed no immediate rules on insurers.
